extracted.intended_audience: law students, lawyers, publishers, printers, booksellers and librarians (United Kingdom, historical statutory context)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes statutory duties, privileges, penalties and procedural rules governing the printing, registration and distribution of books, periodicals and court reports in the United Kingdom (historical statutes as explained in a legal treatise). Useful for publishers, printers, booksellers, librarians and lawyers needing the statutory requirements and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title entry of every book (time limits and penalty)
rubrics_metrics.description: That the title to every book which is published shall be entered within one calendar month from the day of publication, if published in London; and within three calendar months for those books which are published in any other part of the British dominions, under a penalty of five pounds, and the price of eleven copies; to be recovered in an action at law by the managers of the public libraries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to make the entry does not affect the copyright but only subjects the publisher to the penalty. For every entry two shillings is to be paid. The register book may be consulted on payment of one shilling, and a certificate of an entry is to be granted for one shilling. If the clerk refuses or neglects to make the entry or to give a certificate, an advertisement in the Gazette will have the same benefits attached to it, and the clerk will forfeit twenty pounds to the proprietor of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entry requirement for magazines/periodicals
rubrics_metrics.description: In making entries at Stationers' Hall of magazines, reviews, or other periodical publications, it is sufficient to make the entry within one month next after the publication of the first number or volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This special rule treats a periodical's initial issue as the registerable event rather than each issue; statutory citation noted (54 Geo. III. c. 156, s.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal deposit — delivery of copies to public libraries
rubrics_metrics.description: Eleven copies of every book of the largest impression, with all its maps and prints, should, on demand being made thereof in writing within one twelve months of the publication, be delivered by the publisher to the warehouse-keeper (or a person authorized) for the use of specified libraries (British Museum, Sion College, Bodleian, Cambridge public, four Scottish Universities, Trinity College Dublin, King's Inn Library Dublin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warehouse-keeper must deliver the books within one month afterwards to the keeper of the respective libraries or authorized persons. Publishers are liable to a penalty of five pounds, besides the value of it, for every copy not so delivered, received, and handed over. The warehouse-keeper must transmit correct lists every three months of the books entered to the librarians and call on publishers for demanded copies. A publisher may deliver directly to librarians and obtain a receipt equivalent to delivery to the warehouseman. A second edition is not to be delivered unless it contains additions and alterations (nor if the additions are delivered separately). Court holdings show delivery obligations may exist notwithstanding failure to enter title at Stationers' Hall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warehouse-keeper duties and penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: The warehouse-keeper of the Company of Stationers is directed every three months to transmit correct lists of the books entered to the librarians of the eleven public libraries and to call on the publishers for as many copies as are demanded; and to deliver demanded books to the keepers or authorized persons within one month.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure by the warehouse-keeper to duly deliver exposes the publishers and warehouseman to a penalty of five pounds, besides the value, for every copy not delivered. Publisher delivery to librarians with receipt is equivalent to delivery to warehouseman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universities' privileges to print Bibles, Statutes and Almanacks
rubrics_metrics.description: The Universities of Oxford and Cambridge claim the right to print Bibles and statutes under letters patent and have historically possessed certain privileges relating to almanacks and other works by charter and grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Privileges are claimed under various letters patent (e.g., Elizabeth I) and concurrent authority in some instances with the King's printer. Some royal grants for almanacks were declared void but Parliament compensated universities (e.g., duties on sheet almanacks). The Crown's prerogative copyright in these works has been debated; where patents remain valid, the Universities assert interests in them.

rubrics_metrics.name: University exception for bequeathed books and registration after gift
rubrics_metrics.description: Universities are to have for ever the sole liberty of printing books that have been given or bequeathed to them (or which shall thereafter, not being then published, be given to them) for the purpose of appropriating profits for educational uses, subject to conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exception extends only to their own books while printed at the college press and for their sole benefit; any delegation of the right forfeits the privilege. Universities can sell or dispose of copyrights bequeathed to them. Books must be registered at Stationers' Hall within two months after any such gift comes to the officers' knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts' privilege to control publication of judicial proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Courts of Justice claim and exercise a control over the publication of their own proceedings, not on grounds of copyright but on the principle necessary for the due and impartial administration of the laws; such privilege may justify orders restraining publication and injunctions against unauthorized printers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The House of Lords has treated publication of its proceedings as its exclusive privilege and may authorize printing by order while restraining others (cases like Bathurst v. Kearsley and Gurney v. Longman discussed). Reporting by indulgence has been allowed but publishing contrary to orders or bench intimation can be contempt of court (e.g., Observer fined £500). The power aims to prevent ex parte statements detrimental to fair trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privileged restraint by Privy Council, Courts of Law, Mayor's Court, and coroners
rubrics_metrics.description: Apart from the House of Lords, similar privileges have been asserted/exercised by the Privy Council, Courts of Law, the Mayor of London, and in relation to coroner's inquests to restrain publication in the interest of justice and public policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include injunctions to restrain publication of Privy Council matters and trials ordered by the Lord Mayor; a criminal information will lie for publishing an ex parte statement of coroner's inquest because it prejudices subsequent juries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on publishing ex parte coroner's inquest accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: A criminal information will lie for publishing an ex parte statement of the proceedings upon a coroner's inquest; such publication is considered highly prejudicial as it presents evidence without opportunity for cross-examination and may bias juries who decide later trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges have described the publication of inquest proceedings as 'a matter of great criminality' and liable to prosecution to protect the fairness of subsequent trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to give notice of possession/use of a printing press
rubrics_metrics.description: Every person having a printing press or types for printing must give a notice thereof, signed in the presence of and attested by one witness, to the clerk of the peace of the place in which it is intended to be used, who will grant a certificate; the clerk transmits an attested copy to the Secretary of State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An omission in giving such notice, or using the press in any other place than named, subjects the printer to a forfeiture of £20. Letter-founders must give similar notice and keep accounts of types and presses sold, producible on justice's demand under penalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printer's name and residence must be printed on publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon the front of every paper, and upon the first and last leaves of every paper or book which consists of more than one leaf, the printer, whether done gratis or for money, must in legible characters print his name, and that of the city, town, parish, or place, with the name of the street, lane, court or place in which his usual place of abode is situated, under a penalty for every copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The offender is not liable to more than twenty-five penalties with respect to any number of copies of one paper or book (cap on penalties). Statutory references: 39 Geo. III. c.79, s.27 etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printer must record employer and retain copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon a copy of every paper that is printed the printer must write the name and place of abode of his employer, keep it for six calendar months, and produce it to any justice who within that term may require to see it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to do so is punishable by a penalty of twenty pounds for each omission. This record aids prosecution/enforcement and identification of responsible parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to the printing-name/address regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations requiring printer's name/residence do not extend to impressions of engravings; or to printing by letter-press names, address, business or profession of any person and the articles in which he deals; or to papers for sale of estate or goods by auction; nor to alter the regulations respecting newspapers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also, regulations do not extend to require the printer's name or residence to be printed on bank notes, bills of exchange, promissory notes, bonds, deeds, agreements, transfers of public funds, legal proceedings printed by authority, or similar documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of certain offensive subjects and penalties for printers
rubrics_metrics.description: Many subjects offensive to morality and the government must not be printed. A printer is liable to a penalty of £100 for printing certain prohibited items (e.g., relating to insurances on marriages, births, christenings, or certain 'offices' such as sales of gloves, fans, cards, numbers, Her Majesty's picture for improvement of small sums), and to £50 for printing proposals for gambling in the lottery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prosecution may be instituted against the printer as well as against the author and publisher of a libel, whether libel be of an individual or of a blasphemous or seditious nature (statutory references cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Printers' and publishers' liability for libel and seditious/blasphemous material
rubrics_metrics.description: A printer may be prosecuted as well as the author and publisher for printing a libel, including blasphemous or seditious material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law treats printers as responsible parties; booksellers who knowingly sell such pirated or libellous works may likewise be subject to penalties and prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper-specific rules and responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: There are particular statutory rules governing the method by which a newspaper is to be printed and the responsibility of every person engaged in its publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text references stamp and imprint requirements and that persons involved in newspaper publication have been examined with respect to responsibility; printers may need to lodge affidavits at the stamp office or have their name/place printed to recover payment in certain circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of non-compliance on printer's recovery for work
rubrics_metrics.description: It is doubtful whether a printer can recover in an action for work and labour for printing a work on the first and last leaves of which his name and place of abode are not printed according to the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases are cited where failure to comply with statutory formalities (e.g., stamp office affidavits, or printing required details) prevented recovery for printing and publication of periodical works; compliance affects right to payment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printer's lien and commercial duties regarding parts published at different times
rubrics_metrics.description: A printer is not by custom bound to insure for the bookseller the paper of the work, and he has a lien on the latter parts of a work published at different times for the printing of the first parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Custom does not require the printer to bear certain commercial risks; the printer's lien may secure payment for work already supplied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary enforcement powers and penalties for printing offences
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person to whom a paper not printed according to statute is offered for sale may take the offender before a magistrate who may determine guilt and mitigate the penalty. A justice of the peace may, on information on oath, authorize search and seizure of presses, types, and printed papers. Justices may enforce penalties summary up to £20, levy by distress and sale, or commit offender to House of Correction 3–6 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All prosecutions for penalties are to be commenced within three months after penalty is incurred; one moiety of recovery goes to the king, the other to the informer. Appeals from justices' determinations lie to the Quarter Sessions within set timeframes (notice requirements apply). Penalties exceeding £20 may be recovered by action of debt in courts of record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Booksellers' liability for buying, selling and importing pirated works
rubrics_metrics.description: The vendor of a pirated work destroys literary property; penalties are inflicted on those who print and import books protected by the statutes, and booksellers who knowingly sell such works are liable to the same penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory exception: nothing in the act extended to prohibit importing, vending or selling books in Greek, Latin, or any other foreign language printed beyond the seas. Importation of books reprinted abroad first composed in Great Britain is prohibited under forfeiture, penalty of £5 and double the value of the books; later statutes increased penalties and provided rewards to customs officers. Export generally allowed if duties upon paper and bindings have been paid; special rules for university presses and foreign-language works; two penalties may be incurred in the same day for multiple sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bookseller liability for libellous stock
rubrics_metrics.description: The circumstance of buying a libel in the shop of a known bookseller is sufficient prima facie evidence to convict him of the publication; booksellers are thus materially affected by libel laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Booksellers need to exercise care about the contents of works they sell; statutory and case law treat sale in a known bookshop as evidence of publication for libel prosecutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal limits and effects of importation/printing statutes on copyright
rubrics_metrics.description: Under certain importation statutes it is immaterial whether the author's copyright is extinct or not if the book has not been reprinted in England within twenty years; such books may be treated as importable subject to statutory conditions and penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutes (e.g., 12 Geo. II c.36 and later sections) prohibit importation of books reprinted abroad within a statutory period and provide penalties (forfeiture and monetary) and enforcement by customs; commissioners may reward officers for seizing such books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative remedies for recovery of penalties and appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Penalties under printing statutes are subject to summary proceedings before justices, can be mitigated by them, or if exceeding statutory thresholds recovered by action in courts of record; appeals lie to Quarter Sessions with notice and time limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One moiety of recovered penalty goes to the king and the other to the informer (where applicable). Appeals require six days' notice of appeal and must be brought within statutory timeframes (twenty days after determination to the next Quarter Sessions).
